questions.q: What invokes a Lambda function's handler?
options: A trigger — an event source such as an API call, an S3 file landing, or a schedule
A continuously running server process you manage
A manual click in the AWS console every time
A cron job running inside the Lambda function itself
questions.explain: Lambda functions are invoked by trigger events; there's no server sitting idle waiting for work between invocations.

questions.q: What is the maximum execution time for a single Lambda invocation?
options: 15 minutes (900 seconds)
1 hour
24 hours
There is no maximum
questions.explain: Every Lambda function has a hard timeout ceiling of 15 minutes, configurable up to that limit.

questions.q: How do you configure a Lambda function's CPU allocation?
options: You can't set it directly — CPU scales proportionally with the memory setting
You set CPU and memory independently as two separate values
CPU is fixed at one vCPU for every function regardless of memory
CPU allocation is determined by the function's programming language
questions.explain: Lambda only exposes a memory setting (128 MB to 10,240 MB); CPU allocation scales automatically with it, making memory a real performance lever.

options: AWS initializing a fresh execution environment for the first invocation after a period of no traffic
A function running out of memory mid-execution
A trigger firing twice for the same event
The function exceeding its 15-minute timeout
questions.explain: A cold start happens when there's no already-initialized environment to reuse, so AWS has to set one up before the handler runs.

questions.q: How does Lambda billing work between invocations?
options: You're billed only for the milliseconds your code actually executes; nothing runs or is billed between invocations
You pay a flat hourly rate whether or not the function is invoked
You pay only once, when the function is first deployed
Billing is based on the number of lines of code in the handler
questions.explain: Lambda has no idle server to pay for — cost is tied to actual execution time per invocation, not to time spent waiting for triggers.
